title: Early Scottish records
standfirst: The early Scottish records anchor the search for one extended Glasgow family. The next task is to connect its oldest documented households, retaining tentative joins with their evidence and open questions.
question: How can the earliest Glasgow branches be joined into the shared paternal family?
answer: Start with the 1447–1455 Glasgow burgess, the Stirling John of 1475–1480, Alan in the late-fifteenth-century justice record, and the Saltmarket family. The Saltmarket John-to-William property succession is the leading father hypothesis, followed by a proved father–son generation. These working connections guide a single-family reconstruction while the missing identities and generations are tested. The local working tree now selects the Stirling John as an uncertain father of the Saltmarket candidate and, more tentatively, Alan Glasgw. The imported John profile’s identity and Alan’s exact collateral degree remain open.

chapters.title: Glenarm and Stevenston: two selected uncertain fathers
body: Select Robert Glaskow of Larne, Glasgow-3970, as the very low-confidence working father of Elizabeth Glasgow-3961, the Eliz Glascho at Glenarm Town in 1669. Robert is an older recorded adult at Larne in 1653, and the existing uncertain paternal family already includes John Glasgow-3913 and James Glasgow-1081, the adjacent Jo/James Glascho householders at Kilwaughter in the same 1669 roll. Elizabeth shares their unusual recorded Glascho form and the east-Antrim setting. Her assumed adult-householder generation in 1669 can be a daughter generation of the earlier Larne man. This extends an existing local family explanation rather than inventing an unnamed father; no record calls Elizabeth his daughter or John’s sister.

Glenarm Town and Kilwaughter Demesne are distinct places in neighbouring lower and upper Glenarm baronies, not one household or consecutive entries. Elizabeth’s forename, surname form and regional date pattern support a family comparison but do not distinguish daughter from sister, niece, cousin or unrelated namesake. The tax entry does not state whether Glasgow was her birth or married surname, whether she was a widow, or her age. A wife/widow identity within another Glasgow household therefore remains possible. Her circa-1650 birth and the competing before-about-1648 adult estimate are inferences, not ages that establish a generation. The Larne man’s possible identity with the 1618 Scottish child remains uncertain, as do his existing Kilwaughter sons and his own selected Scottish parents. No mother is selected for Elizabeth; neither the elder Jonet Cunningham nor the younger Janet Cunningham is transferred to her as mother. Existing chronology, the possible James identities and the hearsay status of the Larne allegations remain unchanged.

Select John Glasgow-3375, the father associated with Barbara Alason/Allason at Kilwinning in 1679 and 1689, as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-4170, father with Mary Auld at Stevenston in 1717–1718. This is a low/very low-confidence regional household placement. The recorded couple supplies a compatible parent generation, and their son John Glasgow-1434, indexed at Kilwinning in 1679, is already a possible identity for the John who had children with Margaret Cowan at Stevenston in 1701 and 1706. That existing route gives a specific neighbouring-parish family comparison for James’s later Stevenston household. The preferred provisional model places James alongside that John as a possible paternal brother. It does not identify a baptism for James or claim that the 1717–1718 entries name his parents.

James’s before-1698 birth is an existing estimated adult boundary from his 1717 fatherhood, not a baptism or an age. His actual birth could fit a child of the Kilwinning couple, but the route also depends on the unproved identification of their 1679 son with the Stevenston adult. The John-3375 and Rev. John-1073 profiles remain possible accounts of one man; no merge, duplicate resolution, ministry or new son of the minister is established here. The shared John-1604 parent and older family scaffold remain uncertain. The already selected uncertain son James-3105, father at Kilwinning in 1689 with Margaret Park, is a serious surviving identity alternative for James-4170: an earlier Park household followed by a later Auld household is possible, but no occupation, age or marriage bridge identifies them. Retain both accounts without counting the father selection as proof of two distinct James sons. Other local fathers, including the older Matthew of Pyperheugh as a possible father or earlier kinsman, remain alternatives; his 1665 spouse entry alone supplies no James child, and the long interval to 1717 requires caution. No mother is selected for James: Barbara’s known maternity of the 1679 child does not establish James’s mother, and no marriage to Mary Auld is invented beyond the recorded parent pair.

Two newly selected uncertain fathers using existing records and household comparisons; no new mother, original-source inspection, certainty upgrade, identity merge or live WikiTree save. Existing vital dates, age assumptions, source readings and earlier pending amendments remain intact. The two suggested paternal-sibling relationships depend on the selected fathers and the older uncertain identity/parent links; they are not independent sibling attestations. Connectivity counts retained profile accounts, so possible duplicates remain a limitation of the working score.

chapters.period: 1618–1665 · two uncertain fathers and one uncertain mother
chapters.title: Stevenston and South Leith: selected uncertain families
body: Select John Glasgow-1030 as the very low-confidence working father of Matthew Glasgow-3538 of Pyperheugh, Stevenston. John and Jonet Mathie married in Glasgow on 25 January 1618 and have recorded children in the following decade. A son of that household, born in the 1620s, could be an adult spouse in the 1665 testament index that names Matthew. This is a compatible generation, not a new birth estimate. The existing Mathie–Glasgow network supplies a positive social route between Glasgow and Stevenston: David Mathy and Robert Glasgow were co-witnesses in 1554, while Matthew Glasgow and John Mathie were together at Ardeer Nether in 1559–60. The later marriage joins those surname networks. The recurrence of Matthew in the same parish makes this existing household a useful selected descent hypothesis; it does not identify a father in a record.

No inspected record names Matthew’s parents or connects his Pyperheugh household directly to the Glasgow couple. The route depends on Jonet’s unproved place in the older Mathie network and on the probable identification of the 1618 husband with Ninian’s brother John represented by Glasgow-1030. John’s confident Robert Glasgow-1096 father assessment remains conditional on that adult identification and is not newly upgraded. Other Stevenston fathers, collateral descent from the 1559–60 Matthew, and an unrelated same-name family remain possible. The 106-year interval rules out identity with that earlier adult; no missing generation is invented and no direct father edge to him is selected. The Saltcoats sailor John, spouse of Isobell Gray, remains a separate record-defined household; this model does not merge them. The 1619 baptismal witness Mathew Will is not Matthew Mathie or proof of a Glasgow relative.

Assess Jonet Mathie-159 separately as Matthew’s uncertain working mother. Her recorded 1618 marriage and maternity in the following decade provide an actual couple and a compatible childbearing generation; her circa-1597 birth is an estimate. The Mathie associations in Stevenston are the proposed route for this household’s connection to Pyperheugh. Selecting her is a conditional couple hypothesis, not an automatic consequence of attaching John. It has very low confidence: no record calls Matthew her son, no Mathie ancestor is newly attached, and another mother remains possible. The paternal and maternal selections share the same network argument and are correlated, not two independent confirmations.

Select William Glasgow-3075, the Leith mealmaker, as the low-confidence working father of Margaret Glasgow-3186, indexed marrying George Lyell at South Leith on 28 November 1633. William’s household is documented at Leith, with a proposed 10 July 1610 local marriage and a son Archibald baptised in 1618, securely linked to the adult mealmaker by the 1639 apprenticeship and 1647 service of heir. A daughter marrying in 1633 fits that established household generation. Shared surname, the same parish and a coherent marriage/child generation favour this named household over a newly invented father. No source calls Margaret his daughter. Her circa-1610 birth remains an inherited estimate and supplies no independent evidence of William’s paternity.

Retain the strongest specific alternative: Betham’s pedigree of Archibald Glasgow, Rathmalton clerk, whose will was dated April 1673, names Margaret as his only daughter, wife of an unnamed Cairns and mother of Thomas Cairns. The documentary father–daughter relationship is explicit, but identifying that Margaret with Glasgow-3186 remains unproved. A first Lyell marriage in 1633 permits a later Cairns marriage. The preferred William placement avoids requiring that unproved Scottish–Irish identity and remarriage. It also avoids tension with the probable identification of Archibald Glasgow-1101 as the child baptised in Glasgow in 1614 and the 1635 graduate: that child would be an implausible father of a 1633 bride. This is a ranking consideration, not an exclusion: the Scottish identity is unproved, and a baptism is not necessarily an infant’s birth. The new uncertain William field must not be used as a concrete father conflict to reject the Rathmalton candidate. A different South Leith Glasgow father also remains possible. No mother is selected: Catherine Fraith/Fraser’s 1610 bride identity and Christian Scot’s separate Glasgow household remain qualified. William’s testament names Archibald as lawful son and sole executor, not only child; omission of Margaret neither excludes her nor proves kinship.

Margaret’s copied source string records the 28 November 1633 South Leith marriage, OPR 692/2, 90/264, FR3038. Its truncated surname string ASGOWE is retained in the profile comparison, not silently expanded as an original-image reading. The old exact-looking birth year is displayed as circa 1610, an inherited estimate with no age record. South Leith is the marriage place, not an evidenced death place; death date and place remain unknown. Matthew’s before-1650 birth remains uncertain, and his inherited Stevenson birthplace is not proved by the Stevenston residence. The 24 April 1665 date belongs to Jonet Cowan’s testament-index entry, not Matthew’s birth, marriage or death. No original source was newly inspected.

chapters.title: Quothquan and Thankerton: two uncertain fathers
body: Select Stephen Glasgow-1029 as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3910. James’s weaver occupation and Quothquan locality favour using the 1612 court defender and the 1624 testator as one working adult account. Stephen is documented as an adult in Glasgow in 1575 and with wife Margaret Grahame in 1582; his approximate 1550 birth is an estimate, not a birth record. The existing tree already places John Glasgow-3296, the 1650 Quothquan testator, under Stephen, uncertain. The preferred model treats the two early Quothquan men as paternal brothers rather than making the later John James’s father. A Stephen born around the mid-sixteenth century could have fathered James in the 1570s–1590s and John in a similar generation. This uses a named family already connected to Quothquan, at very low confidence, rather than inventing a missing parent. No record names Stephen as James’s father or James and John as brothers.

The route depends both on the proposed James–John brotherhood and on John’s already uncertain Stephen parentage. The Glasgow–Montfoid–Mid Calder–Quothquan identities are not proved migrations. John’s 1650 testament names his sister Bessie and no child or parent; omission of James, already dead by 1624, does not disprove brotherhood. John himself could instead be James’s father if older than his inherited estimate, or the men could be uncle/nephew, cousins or unrelated local namesakes. The older John and Thomas tenants in the 1520s–1530s remain possible ancestral relatives with unproved intervening generations; no direct father edge to them is selected. Margaret Grahame is Stephen’s documented spouse in 1582, not a documented mother of James, so no mother is attached. John’s existing mother field and all earlier parent and identity alternatives remain unchanged.

Select the Quothquan weaver James Glasgow-3910 as the uncertain working father of Helen Glasgow-3909, the married Thankerton woman whose testament was indexed in January 1627. The shared uncommon surname, neighbouring Quothquan/Thankerton locality and an adult weaver recorded at the 1612 hearing followed by a married woman dead by 1627 give a coherent father/daughter generation. Helen’s circa-1605 birth is an inherited estimate, not her stated age; it is compatible with a James born before the mid-1590s but is not independent proof of that generation. This is a low-confidence local family selection. No inspected record calls Helen James’s daughter.

Helen could instead be James’s sister or niece, a daughter of the later John or another local Glasgow. Neither testament index supplies her age, children or parents. Thankerton is her household’s stated residence, not a proved birthplace or death place. Margaret Threipland’s 1626 Quothquan widow entry remains a possible wife for James, not a selected spouse identity and not a mother for Helen. Both newly considered mothers remain unknown. The original 1624 and 1627 testaments are discriminating follow-up evidence, not a prerequisite for displaying these qualified working links.

The circa-1605 birth estimate is replaced locally by an explicitly conditional adult-role estimate, before 1595: this assumes an age of at least 18 at the 1612 hearing and the preferred same-weaver identification. Neither the record nor the profile supplies a real age, so this is not a recorded birthday or a hard biological exclusion. The 1607–1608 acts concern the earlier dispute, not a newly established birth or exact adult-age observation. The 26 July 1624 date is a testament confirmation, so death is shown as before that date and its place is left unresolved; Quothquan is the stated residence. Imported profile values remain in the comparison and the earlier biography is retained as history.

Identification with the distinct weaver indexed at Back of Lindsaylands in 1680 would exclude a death before 1624 if established, but that later identity is itself only possible. Retain Glasgow-3910 as the record-defined 1624 account for the selected uncertain family; do not merge the profiles or transfer Glasgow-3332’s unproved parent and child attachments. Those existing family fields remain unchanged, and the proposed Stephen placement is an alternative to that account’s current pedigree.

chapters.title: Michael of Irvine and James of Kirknewton: two working fathers
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1512 as Michael Glasgow-1406’s uncertain working father. This activates a parent comparison already recorded in Michael’s profile. Robert is a record-defined Ayr father with Margaret Donald in 1670 and 1671; Michael is recorded as an Irvine skinner in 1679 and is already treated locally as the later saddler/councillor. Robert’s before 1652 birth is an upper-bound estimate from his later children, not evidence that he was born in 1652. Michael’s before 1679 boundary likewise does not date his birth. An older Robert and a Michael born well before the summons could fit a father/son generation; their ages are not recorded. The regional family setting and existing candidate justify a very low-confidence working choice. No record names Michael’s father, and no shared occupation, holding, witness or household identifies this Robert as his parent.

John Glasgow-1604 is another viable older father generation, rather than a disproved alternative. Robert’s own attachment to that John is unproved, and taking John’s approximate 1626 date narrowly could press the generation spacing if Robert had Michael early. Those older dates and attachments remain hypotheses; no date is adjusted to repair the pedigree. Another Ayrshire father, or a sibling/collateral relationship to Robert, remains possible. Margaret Donald-1722 is named in Robert’s 1670–1671 children’s records, not in a record naming Michael’s mother. She is not selected as Michael’s mother. The existing 1679 skinner/later saddler/councillor identification is inherited from the completed merge, not newly proved; keep the 1679 summons,1686/1702 civic records and 1699/1701 leather-work references distinct in their evidence roles. Elizabeth Garven and Catharine Baird remain the recorded mothers in Michael’s later child group. The 1700 Elizabeth entry has an assumed year and no proved 1 January birthday. No mother, marriage or death date is newly inferred for Michael, and the 1700–1715 household chronology does not itself identify his parents. The earlier proof-level hold on Robert is retained as history, not treated as a disproof of this qualified local model.

Select the older William Glasgow-1026 as James Glasgow-3526’s uncertain working father. William’s Kirknewton household is documented by Bessie in 1682 and William in 1705. James is the father-name account behind John’s 1717 Kirknewton/East Calder entry, with a Helen 1714 association held in a collaborative tree. James’s 1688 birth is an unsupported profile estimate. If the rough 1660/1688 generations are close, William would have been about 28 at his birth, and the proposed son falls between William’s already recorded children. This same-area, compatible household generation is preferred provisionally, at low confidence. The combined Kirknewton/East Calder label does not establish the exact historic parish or continuous residence, and no record names William as James’s father.

John-3525’s earlier biography links its father to James Glasgow-1547, whereas the maintained local family uses James-3526. The 1717 index names James, not either modern profile ID. James-1547, associated with Andrew Glasgow-1546 and a 1702 entry, remains a surviving alternative childhood identity for the adult father. If baptised as an infant in 1702 he would be about 15 in 1717 and about 12 at Helen’s tree-held 1714 date. That makes the ordinary older-William model more straightforward, but neither a later childhood baptism nor an erroneous Helen association is excluded. No merge or categorical biological exclusion is selected. Andrew-1546 therefore remains an alternative father through that identity, not a newly attached parent. Andrew-1319 or another older Calder father remains possible. William-3974, the separate 1671 child of Andro, would imply younger fatherhood at a literal 1688 birth; the date estimates alone do not exclude him. Do not undo the split between that child and the older William-1026. The already attached Irish James-1025 may be another account of this James, a relative or an unrelated namesake. Sharing a proposed father does not prove two distinct James sons, and no Scottish-to-Tyrone identity or migration is established. Ann McCook is not selected as James’s mother, and Christian Cook’s attachment to James-1547 is not transferred. James’s wife and the two children’s mothers remain unknown. Helen’s exact 1714 date and father association are tree-held, not an inspected baptism. John’s 1717 record supplies a father name but not a birth or parents for the adult James. The existing child-parent grades, James’s estimated 1688 field, William’s selected uncertain John-3610 father and all older alternatives are preserved.

Both are selected uncertain local father models using existing material. Neither adult receives a mother. No original newly inspected, source-record discovery, identity merge, live WikiTree edit or confidence upgrade is claimed. Existing dates, places and attached relatives are retained; connectivity counts profile accounts, including possible duplicates and older uncertain links.

chapters.period: 1676–1699 · two uncertain fathers and one mother
chapters.title: Kilwinning and Irvine: the remaining early family heads
body: Select John Glasgow-3375 as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-3105. James is the combined working father account behind the two 1689 Kilwinning child entries, one naming Margaret Park. John is a record-defined father in that same parish in 1679 and 1689, associated with Barbara Alason/Allason. The rough 1650 and 1670 family generations would put John at about twenty when James was born, and both generations could have children recorded during 1689. Neither year is a recorded birth; John’s captured before-about 1661 boundary is an adult-status estimate and permits an earlier birth. No date is changed to fit this placement. Prefer this recorded local adult as a provisional parent-generation anchor over assigning James directly to the older John-1604 scaffold or to an otherwise unidentified father. The shared parish and compatible generational spacing supply the logic, at very low confidence; no source names James as John’s son.

John-1604 remains a possible older father rather than a rejected alternative. His approximate 1626 birth and 1664 death are unsourced; a literal 1670 James birth would conflict with that death estimate, requiring at least one estimate to be wrong. Neither is silently adjusted. Hew-1066 or another local Glasgow remains possible; the current shortlist is not exhaustive. John-3375 may be the same man as the minister John-1073. If so, the minister’s approximate 1653 generation would imply younger parenthood around 1670, still dependent on James’s unrecorded birth. No merge, proved brotherhood, ministerial occupation for John-3375 or new father for the minister is inferred. John’s own attachment to John-1604 and the older Hugh-1603 scaffold retain their existing uncertainty. Barbara Alason is the recorded/probable mother of John’s known children, not a newly selected mother of James. James’s mother stays unknown. Margaret Park is recorded for the July 1689 child; Anne’s May 1689 index omits a mother. The combined James father account and the two children’s sibling status remain provisional. Two index/baptism dates two months apart do not prove two births to one mother. No witness, occupation, property or inheritance bridge ties James to John.

Select Hew Glasgow-1066 and Margaret Lachland-2 as the uncertain working father and mother of Hugh Glasgow-3109, the Irvine father with Jean Service in 1696, through the existing strong possible identity with their 1676 Kilwinning child Hew Glasgow-1067. If baptised near birth, the child would have been about twenty in 1696. The name variant Hew/Hugh, compatible generation and neighbouring Ayrshire parish setting make this a practical preferred childhood comparison. This activates a comparison already explicitly retained in both profiles, rather than treating the 1696 child’s entry as the adult father’s birth. Maternity is assessed independently from the 1676 child clause: the supplied Scotland’s People index explicitly names Margaret Lachland with Hew Glasgow. The Findmypast transcript abbreviates/queries her name as Mt Lach?. Margaret is not selected merely because she is Hew’s spouse. Both adult parent links depend on the uncertain childhood identity and remain uncertain; the child’s recorded parentage is not proof of the adult’s origins.

Keep Glasgow-1067 and Glasgow-3109 as separate profile accounts of a possible single man. The shared parents do not establish two distinct sons called Hew/Hugh. No record joins the 1676 child to the 1696 Irvine father or proves the proposed sequence from Jean Service to Mary Dean from 1699; no death, remarriage or continuous personal identifier has been supplied. The Mary Dean family retains its own unproved childhood-to-adult identification. The older Hew-1066 himself is a possible alternative identity of the 1696 father, rather than simultaneously being his proved father. That alternative would invalidate the selected child identity and the maternal transfer; it is not materialised alongside them. A different unrecorded Hugh remains possible. The 1677 preacher has no inspected residence or kin bridge here; the selected 1676 child could not have been that adult preacher a year later. The 1751 Irvine/London sailor remains an unselected occupational identity, not an event newly assigned to either account. Retain the literal source discrepancies: the official supplied index and Findmypast give24 May 1676, while the older father biography reports5 May from FamilySearch. A24 May marriage is also reported in that family biography; the original page and event type were not re-read. No baptism, birthday or ceremony date is newly corrected or proved. Hugh-3109’s before-about 1676 boundary remains an estimate, not a birth record or a hard exclusion of the 1676 child. Existing Jean Service co-parentage, both 1696 children, Mary Dean associations and the child’s parent-field grades are retained. No relationship-certainty change is counted. Margaret is not assigned to any other child whose record does not name her.

These are selected uncertain working relationships using existing material, not new original-record discoveries. No vital date, location, existing spouse or attached relative is cleared, and no identity merge, live WikiTree save or confidence upgrade is claimed. Counts concern retained profile accounts and inherit uncertainty and possible duplicates in older links.

chapters.title: Two Lothian family heads: the Duffe and Kirknewton households
body: Select Johnne Glasgow-1151 as the uncertain working father of James Glasgow-2682, husband of Isobell Duffe. James’s captured biography already proposes Johnne as a possible father. The Inveresk and Musselburgh index records Johnne on25 November 1632 with father Alexander Glasgow. James and Isobell’s Edinburgh children begin with Jean on13 April 1677. If Johnne was baptised near birth and James’s approximate 1655 birth is close, Johnne would have been about 23 at James’s birth and 44 at the first known grandchild’s baptism. This is an ordinary father/son generation within the wider Lothian setting. Select that already recorded comparison provisionally, at very low confidence. Neither James’s own birth nor Johnne’s adult life is established; this is a parent-generation model, not a source naming James’s father.

James Glasgow-3076, recorded at St Cuthbert’s in 1661 with father James Glasgow-3077 and mother Annapill Glessie, remains an alternative childhood identity explicitly suggested in that child’s profile. If baptised as an infant he would have been about 16 at Jean’s 1677 baptism; that younger parenthood makes it less straightforward than the selected ordinary-generation model, but does not exclude him. An older-child baptism also remains possible. John Glasgow-1084 is another previously proposed father. His Gordon/Berwickshire household and separate James Glasgow-3107 account remain viable comparisons; no missing death or marriage is treated as an exclusion. A different unrecorded father remains possible, and the shortlist is not exhaustive. No source joins Johnne’s 1632 child record to an adult father of James, supplies James’s age, or connects their households by craft, witness, property or inheritance. The preference is weak, based on the existing candidate, chronology and regional fit; the component gain supplies no identity evidence. No mother is selected for James. Johnne’s index names Alexander but no mother; his existing Clerk attachment does not establish a mother for James. Keep the Duffe household distinct from the Edinburgh weaver Glasgow-1150 and the unresolved Whitecastle James Glasgow-1376. The old 1657 event on1376 names James as father of Marione, not as the child. That role error does not supply a birth or parentage for the Duffe husband. The old reference to “James-1168,about1540” also mislabels the Corsankell elder; the selected route instead uses Johnne’s actual recorded father Alexander Glasgow-1148. The 1679 and 1680 sons called James remain separate child accounts; no infant death or survivor marrying Jean Dobie is newly established. The 1679 mother’s indexed Elizabeth/Isobell Duffe difference remains an existing household-identity qualification. All six children, spouse, dates and previous assessments are preserved.

Select John Glasgow-3610 as the uncertain working father of William Glasgow-1026, the older Kirknewton householder associated with Ann McCook by 1682. This activates the same-parish candidate already retained in William’s research. A 1649 Kirknewton/East Calder index names Johne Glasgow as the father of the child Johne; the adult account also carries a Margaret comparison with unresolved 1646/1649 dates. A father active in 1649 could have another son around William’s estimated 1660 birth. If the adult John is the 1608 Mid Calder child used in his own selected family model, he would have been about 52 in 1660, chronologically possible for a father. That childhood identity is itself uncertain and is not required for the local parent generation to remain possible. The common parish setting and compatible parent generation favour this existing John comparison over restoring the younger Walter-1554 as William’s father or importing the weak Kilwinning John-1604 comparison. Select John at low confidence. No inspected baptism, marriage, testament or property record names William as this John’s son.

chapters.title: The 1652 Edinburgh cordiner: a working Glasgow childhood
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1027 as the uncertain working father of the Edinburgh cordiner Robert Glasgow-3938 through possible identity with the indexed Glasgow child Robert Glasgow-1078, baptised on 17 November 1618. The published Edinburgh marriage register names Robert as a cordiner with Janet Thomsone on 1 July 1652. The older Robert is the probable identity of the Glasgow cordiner admitted burgess on 22 April 1613 and is the named father of the 1618 child. If baptised near birth, that child would have been about 33 at the July 1652 marriage. The matching name, compatible adult generation and same craft make this a useful preferred family comparison over an otherwise unidentified parent or a more distant cordiner kinsman. The trade association supplies a reason to select the family, but neither hereditary training nor a Glasgow-to-Edinburgh move is documented. The father selection is low confidence; it does not identify the child with the adult as an established fact.

Select Jonet Cunningham-20923 as the independently assessed uncertain mother of the Edinburgh adult only through the same possible childhood identity. The 1618 baptism explicitly names Jonet Conynghame as mother of Robert Glasgow-1078. This is an explicit maternal clause for the child, not an inference from the older Robert’s marriage alone or from a Cunningham surname elsewhere. Its transfer to Glasgow-3938 depends entirely on the uncertain identity and therefore remains uncertain. The father’s craft provides no independent evidence of maternity.

Keep Robert Glasgow-1078, Glasgow-3938 and the Larne Robert Glasgow-3970 as separate profile accounts. Both adult accounts are now provisionally placed in the 1618 child’s family; this does not establish two distinct sons named Robert. The 1652 Edinburgh event and the 1653 Larne account are not simultaneous incompatible events on the available evidence: they could concern one mobile man or different namesakes. Neither a migration nor that combined identity is selected as proved. Robert Glasgow-1149 remains the separate existing candidate for the Euphame Lorimer household. Her indexed children in 1651, 1659, 1662 and 1664 bracket the Thomsone marriage, favouring two Edinburgh men. The reported 1 March 1644 West Port sasine also names Eupham Lorimer and belongs to that household comparison; it does not give a West Port residence or wife to the 1652 bridegroom. The original sasine is uninspected. The 1618 child’s attached younger Cunningham spouse and 1645 James association do not prove his adult identity. A later Thomsone marriage could be a remarriage if that association is correct, but no death or remarriage sequence is supplied. Preserve the existing attachments and all namesake alternatives. Glasgow-3938’s before-1634 birth boundary is an age-derived profile estimate, not a recorded birth. It remains unchanged, as do the child’s baptism, the Larne estimate and all existing spouses, children and confidently marked links. The Edinburgh marriage gives no parents, age or children. No apprentice, burgess, witness, property or migration record joins these accounts. An unrelated cordiner or another son, nephew or cousin in the wider family remains possible. body: Select John Glasgow-1561 as the uncertain working father of George Glasgow-3100 of Campbeltown through possible identity with John’s indexed Linlithgow son George-1560 of 20 January 1622. Prefer this comparison provisionally over the older 1605 Mid Calder George-1082, who would have been about 54 in 1659, without excluding that man. The 1627 Glasgow George-1090 is a close alternative, about 32 in 1659; his profile also carries a separate, unproved Fanne Smith household association requiring its own identity review. The preference is weak and practical: the 1622 child has no established incompatible adult fate, and the household timing is compatible. Missing later records are not positive identity evidence. No shared occupation, holding, spouse, witness or migration record identifies the Linlithgow child with the Campbeltown father. This is a very low-confidence family selection, not an identified migration or a record naming the adult’s father.

Select George Glasgow-3100 as Agnes Glasgow-1562’s uncertain working father. This activates the existing geographic family suggestion: Agnes’s captured profile places her Longwill household in Campbeltown, with a 1670 marriage-year field and a son’s 1683 birth field, while George is the named father in the 1659 Campbeltown event. Their approximate parent/child generations permit an older daughter in that household. The same locality and generation make daughter a useful provisional placement alongside George’s attached James and recorded Alexander. The marriage year, child details and Agnes’s circa-1650 birth are profile-held leads, not a newly inspected parish entry. No source names Agnes’s father; a sister, cousin, other local family or unrecorded father remains possible.

chapters.title: A provisional Glasgow–Larne–Belfast family
body: Select Robert Glasgow-1027 and Jonet Cunningham-20923 as the uncertain working father and mother of Robert Glaskow of Larne, Glasgow-3970, through the existing possible identity with their son Robert Glasgow-1078, baptised at Glasgow on 17 November 1618. The 1653 Larne account gives no age or parents, and its before-1625 birth boundary permits the 1618 child; that child would have been about 23 during the alleged 1641 events and 35 in 1653. The Scottish child has no established later fate that excludes this adult account. Choose the already recorded possible identity as the working family explanation, at low confidence. The baptism names both parents, so the maternal selection is assessed from that same explicit child clause, not from a Cunningham surname association in Ulster. Both adult parent links depend on the uncertain identity and remain uncertain; the baptism’s direct parentage must not be transferred as proof of the Larne man’s origins.

Select Robert of Larne-3970 as Captain James Glasgow-3172’s uncertain working father. This adopts the existing possible son-or-younger-relative comparison: Larne, Belfast and Kilwaughter form the north-east Antrim setting of the recorded Robert and later James, and an older Robert active in 1641–1653 can precede a shipmaster active by 1667. James commanded the Blessing of Saltcoats in the 1667 Macartney correspondence and the James of Belfast in 1679. These are compatible Scottish-west-coast/Antrim associations, not a parent clause. Son is selected over the unresolved younger-relative alternatives for one provisional paternal route; no mother is selected for James.

Robert-1078 and Robert-3970 remain separate profile accounts of a possible single man; the selected parents do not establish two distinct Robert sons or an identity merge. No record joins the 1618 baptism to Larne, supplies the Larne man’s Scottish origin, or rules out another Robert. The 1666 John of Portrush shipmaster is a further possible identity, not an occupation proved for either Robert; the later Robert/Rachel household remains separate. James-3172, the Scottish child James-3971 of 1645, and the Kilwaughter James-1081 may be one, two or three men. All accounts remain; no identity among those James groups is selected. A child baptised in 1645 could have been a shipmaster aged about 22 in 1667, assuming infant baptism, but that is compatibility only. The father named in that 1645 record is not independently identified with the 1618 child. John-3913’s circa-1630 and Captain James’s circa-1640 births are inherited estimates, not dates that establish or exclude a generation. If John’s 1630 were literal and the Larne man were born in 1618, fatherhood at about twelve would be an important chronological objection; both the age estimate and John’s uncertain paternal attachment require testing. No birth year is changed to force the selected route. Captain James could instead be a nephew, other relative, unrelated namesake, or a member of the Saltcoats sailor John-4152’s family; the named Saltcoats vessel makes that a real competing route, not evidence that John was his father. The two women Cunningham-20923 and Cunningham-22604 are distinct: the elder is the named 1618 mother, the younger the named mother in the 1645 James record. Neither that younger maternity nor a marriage to her is transferred to the Larne adult or captain through these selections. The existing uncertain Kilwaughter father links remain uncertain; none becomes proved by joining their supposed ancestor to Scotland. The Larne allegations are hearsay, not a judicial finding of guilt, and the 1686 will reference is not a proved death date. No new original inspection, certainty upgrade, live WikiTree edit or identity merge is claimed. Connectivity counts profile accounts and does not resolve the possible duplicates.

chapters.title: Saltcoats: two proved daughters and a possible earlier father
body: The 1637 testament identifies Glasgow-4152 as sailor in Saltcoats, dead December 1636, father of Glasgow-4151 and Glasgow-4153. These father links were already confident; his omitted catalogue page separated the visible family.

Select John Glasgow-3193, the recorded son at Corsankell in 1571 and probable Kilwinning tenant of 1559–60, as the Saltcoats sailor John Glasgow-4152’s uncertain working father. Saltcoats in Ardrossan adjoins the Stevenston–Kilwinning coastal parish cluster where this earlier Glasgow family is documented. A later-sixteenth-century son of the earlier adult could have been a working sailor and father of two daughters by 1636. The choice gives the Saltcoats household a provisional place in an existing local John line, using geography and a feasible generation. It is a low-confidence selection, not a named parent clause or an identification of the two Johns.

No source names the sailor’s parents or age. His former c.1600 birth was an unsupported creation estimate; it is not replaced by an invented older birth to fit this hypothesis. If a birth near 1600 is eventually established, the earlier John would have been an older father, and a grandson or more distant collateral placement could be more natural. Same given name is weak support and does not distinguish this candidate securely from Glasgow-3921 (James younger), another member of the local family, or an unrecorded father. The sailor could belong elsewhere in that family or to another branch. The 1559–60 Kilwinning attribution to the Corsankell John is itself probable, although the 1571 Corsankell family is directly recorded. The same-person alternative is less economical: an adult in 1559 would have been about 95 or older at the sailor’s death in 1636, assuming adulthood at eighteen. That is an illustrative age comparison, not a proved exclusion. The father-versus-grandfather degree remains open. No mother is assigned to the sailor or to his daughters; Agnes Wilson’s joint tenancy does not make her his mother, and Isobell Gray’s widowhood does not prove her maternity. The girls’ already-proved father links remain proved. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree save or confidence upgrade is made.

chapters.title: Agnes Glasgow: a working daughter of James younger
body: Select James Glasgow younger (Glasgow-3921), the Corsankell tenant, as Agnes’s uncertain working father. Her probable 1601 and compatible 1606 Milneburne sasines and her 1628 Stevenston testament place her in the same small parish as the documented Corsankell family of 1559–1571. James younger’s approximate 1540 generation is a natural fit for the father of a woman already married by 1601. His existing plausible daughters Katherine Glasgow-1495 and Geillis Glasgow-3179 belong to the neighbouring Stevenston–Ardrossan women’s network; Geillis’s 1603 estate also names a James Glasgow in Stevenston in its debts. These are local family comparisons, not proved sisters or identification of the creditor. The earlier James-1168/Margaret Smith placement mixed two generations: Margaret is associated with the younger James, not the elder. Selecting the younger James gives the leading generational placement without inheriting that unsupported mother.

No record names Agnes’s father. Parish, generation and the existing family comparisons support only a low-confidence choice. The 1601 entry is a land-record registration, not a marriage date or an age statement; Agnes may already have been married for many years. As an illustration only, a married woman aged about 20–35 in 1601 would have been born about 1566–1581, making James younger about 26–41 and James elder about 51–66 at her birth. These are comparison assumptions, not birth estimates or exclusions. James elder remains an alternative father if Agnes was older. Edward Glasgow-1557 or another local Glasgow remains an alternative, especially if the unproved sisterhood with Jonet Glasgow-1494 is established. Edward’s own approximate 1570 birth makes that father generation less comfortable for a woman already married in 1601, but the estimate is not a hard conflict.

Neither the two women’s sisterhood nor the two Logan husbands’ brotherhood is documented. Under the selected James-younger father and the existing uncertain James → Edward → Jonet chain, Agnes could instead be Jonet’s aunt; that is a conditional model consequence, not a new proved kinship. Margaret Smith is not selected as Agnes’s mother, and her 1632 husband is not proved identical to the Corsankell man. The unnamed Stevenston elder of 1613 remains unidentified. No identity merge or live relationship edit is made.

Agnes’s captured WikiTree birth field is blank. The public c.1610 display was an unsupported inherited estimate and cannot date a woman probably already married in 1601. Her actual birth remains unknown; “before 1601” is a conditional outer boundary from the probable sasine identity. The 1628 testament date is not an exact death date. Stevenston is in Ayrshire; the corrected death locality is an uncertain inference from her stated residence, not a recorded place of death.

One uncertain father joins an existing family. The 1601 year denotes a probable record identity, not a birthday. Measured cohort memberships, the fixed baseline and confident links are preserved; only working connectivity gains the selected edge.

chapters.title: Margaret and Barbara: working daughters of Ninian Glasgow
body: Select daughter from the existing daughter-or-niece comparison with Ninian Glasgow. Margaret married Edinburgh cordiner William Hardie in 1611. Barbara Glasgow married another Edinburgh cordiner in 1616, while Ninian’s documented Glasgow son Robert is probably the cordiner admitted in 1613. Ninian’s possible son William supplies a family route into South Leith. Margaret’s estimated adult generation fits Ninian’s approximate 1550 generation. Together the generation, adjoining Edinburgh–Leith setting and repeated family craft make Ninian’s household the leading existing placement; daughter supplies the simplest provisional degree.

No record names Margaret’s father or proves that she and Barbara were sisters. Niece, another close relative or another local Glasgow family remain alternatives. The cordiners worked in different burghs; a shared trade does not prove one incorporation or apprenticeship. The Robert-cordiner identity and William’s Ninian parentage are supporting inferences. Margaret’s before-1595 birth is an adult-status estimate, not a baptism. Repeated William Hardie marriages do not prove one serial husband or Margaret’s death. No mother is selected.

Select Ninian Glasgow as an uncertain working father within Barbara’s already preferred household or immediate collateral circle. Barbara married Edinburgh cordiner George Johnstoun in 1616; Ninian’s documented Glasgow son Robert is probably the cordiner admitted in 1613, and possible son William lived at South Leith. Barbara’s adult generation fits Ninian’s family. Her possible identity with Barbara Glasgow-3182, the 1611 South Leith bride already tentatively placed as Ninian’s daughter, supplies a second, explicitly conditional route to the same father.

No record names Barbara’s father. Daughter is selected provisionally over niece or another family; trade alone cannot decide the degree. If the 1611 and 1616 brides are one woman, these two Ninian attachments describe one possible daughter twice, not two historical sisters. chapters.title: Three more early family placements, explicitly uncertain
body: The local working tree now selects William of Saltmarket as Michael of Stevenston’s possible father, Andrew of Calder as Jonat Menzeis’s possible father, and Ninian as Barbara Wilson’s possible father. These choices use the existing brother/cousin, same-parish remarriage and daughter/niece comparisons.

Michael Glasgow of Stevenston: The existing Stevenston study places Michael as a probable brother or cousin of James elder of Corsankell, rather than his son. Michael was an adult witness in the Glencairn estate network in 1549; both appear in the same small estate landscape in the 1559–60 teind list. Their approximate 1525 and 1515 generations fit brothers. Select the brother option provisionally and extend James’s already uncertain father William to Michael. This uses an existing older household without inventing an intervening person. The Mathie–Glencairn network supplies a credible route between the burgh family and these estates. Limits: The brother-versus-cousin choice is unresolved, and James’s own father William is uncertain. No record calls Michael William’s son. A cousin through another burgh household, an older generation than the estimated 1525 birth, or a separate family remains possible. Brakpleuch and Dubbs may represent one Michael or two. No mother, exact birth or death is inferred.

Jonat Glasgow, wife of David Menzeis: Jonat is the mother in a Mid Calder baptism in 1609. The existing comparison prefers her possible identity with Jonet Glasgow who married Martin Ramsy in the same parish in 1624, fifteen years later. That Jonet is already placed as Andrew’s testament daughter. Select Andrew as Jonat’s uncertain father through this local identity reconstruction. Her estimated 1585 generation fits Andrew’s household; the same name, parish and feasible remarriage sequence favour this model over the more distant Ninian household. Limits: This combines two uncertain identity steps: the 1609 mother with the 1624 bride, and the bride with Andrew’s testament daughter. David Menzeis’s death and the bride’s widowhood are not recorded in the material reviewed. Jonat and Jonet may be different women; retain both profiles and do not count an identity merge. Ninian Glasgow remains a competing father hypothesis. No mother is attached.

Barbara Glasgow, wife of Johne Wilsoune: The existing branch assessment already favours Barbara as a daughter or niece of Ninian. Her 1611 South Leith marriage entry fits the Leith setting of Ninian’s possible son William and the adjoining Edinburgh craft households; Ninian’s documented son Robert was a cordiner. The estimated 1590 daughter generation fits Ninian’s estimated 1550 generation. Select daughter as the simpler working placement within this already identified household, while retaining niece as an alternative. This is a combined locality, generation and family-network inference. Limits: Neither the marriage entry nor Ninian’s testament names Barbara as his daughter. The proposed Leith brother William is himself uncertain, and shared craft geography is suggestive rather than individual proof. Barbara may instead be Ninian’s niece or belong to another local family. If she is Barbara-567, the existing William-3522 father claim becomes a rival explanation. The adult Barbara identities remain separate, the 1611 date discrepancy stays open, and no mother is assigned.

Each is low confidence and counts only as a selected uncertain parent in the working graph. Keep possible duplicate profiles separate, mothers independent, and the confident graph unchanged. No new source reading is claimed.

chapters.title: Four selected working connections
body: The local working tree now selects Andrew of Calder as tentative father of James, John of Linlithgow and David of Mid Calder. It selects the older Mid Calder/Quothquan John as tentative father of the1640s Kirknewton John. These are logical reconstructions from material already on this site, not newly discovered parentage records.

James Glasgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Andrew’s documented rural Calder household is the preferred working anchor for James’s nearby Mid Calder family. He was alive across the estimated1575–1586 birth interval of all three Lothian fathers; Hermand John’s1577 death would require an earlier birth estimate for David. That favours this coherent provisional family without excluding the other father. Andrew was alive until1598 and the uncertain generations allow James to be an older son. This uses the actual Calder setting and compatible family sequence, not the withdrawn assertion that the testament named James. James’s Inveresk/Fisherrow identity remains a separate uncertainty. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is another plausible older local father. The George named at Mureistoun1586 and the George witness1605 are a competing father/relative lead; identifying that George with merchant1099 would require additional identity assumptions and young fatherhood. None is excluded. Andrew’s omission of James weakens this model; it does not disprove an older son.

John Glasgow of Linlithgow → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: Select the same older Calder household as the working origin for this neighbouring Lothian family. John’s estimated1579 generation and children recorded1613–1622 fit an older son of Andrew, whose own father is tentatively John-1093. The proximity and compatible generations make this a useful shared-family model alongside James and David, rather than an assertion that the three are proved brothers. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 is a compatible alternative if John1561’s estimated birth is earlier than1577. A separate unnamed local father remains possible. Andrew’s1598 testament does not name John; do not restore the obsolete James/Andrew/William child list or attach Jonet Anderson as mother.

David Glasgow of Mid Calder → Andrew Glasgow of Calder: David’s1606 and1612 Mid Calder baptisms place his household in the same small Calder area as the earlier Andrew household. His approximate generation permits Andrew to be his father. The first recorded daughter Elspeth is consistent with the Elizat name in Andrew’s household, a minor naming clue rather than a mother identification. Select Andrew as the tentative shared father with James and John; exact birth years remain estimates. Alternatives: John of Hermand-3181 or another older local Glasgow could be the father. If David’s approximate1586 birth were established, he would have been young when omitted from Andrew’s1598 testament, making that omission more troublesome. It is not an established birth date. Elizat Stevinsoun and the discredited Jonet Anderson attribution are not automatically assigned as mothers.

John Glasgow of Kirknewton → John Glasgow, Mid Calder/Quothquan working identity: The older John already represents the father named in Mid Calder baptisms1608–1609. His son John-1086, baptised1608, is a viable earlier identity for the adult John who had children in neighbouring Kirknewton/East Calder1646–1650: age38 at the1646 birth is straightforward. Select the older John as working father of3610 on that local and chronological reconstruction. Keep the two son profiles separate while testing their possible identity. Alternatives: John-1086 has a later Biggar account that has not been equated with3610. They may be different men, and the older father’s Mid Calder/Montfoid/Quothquan identity is itself uncertain. Robert-4006 is another generationally compatible Calder father. This does not restore the former unsupported William-1087 father or treat1629 as a recorded birthday.
All four edges are uncertain and count only in the working pedigree. Confident relationships, raw WikiTree parent fields and the fixed cohort are unchanged. No mother is assigned by these selections.

chapters.title: Quothquan tenants before the later weaver
body: The full Carnwath court book is publicly readable. Printed passages name Robert and William Glesquho in 1524, John as a Quothquan tenant in 1525/26 and Upper Quothquan in 1531/32, and Thomas Gleschow at Quothquan in 1527/28. John’s later records include a forfeiture decree and an October 1532 malt case.

John and Thomas form a possible early local family group to connect with James Glasgow, the Quothquan weaver documented in 1607–1612 and dead by 1624. No father, spouse or child is named for the early men in the inspected passages. The missing generations remain an explicit research question; the burgh candidates are retained.

Court headings can have wrong years or repeat an event. Dates here follow Dickinson’s cautious Appendix B, including February 1527/28 and the bracketed 1525/26 year. This corrects the former search-only access note; no new paternal join is counted.

The remaining indexed name-bearing passages are now read: Thomas’s repeated entries consolidate into five court meetings, with a March 1528 judgment concerning cultivation and rent prohibitions. No named Glasgow kin or individual tenancy transfer was recovered. The next test is leases and named heirs. The separate Torphichen “Wilyame Glasgow” lead is an index-boundary false hit: Kamis, Wilyame precedes Glasgow the place.
